global_silver_linings.title: Blind Dressage Horse Wins Competitions By Using ‘Equine Braille’
global_silver_linings.snippet: Despite going blind, a remarkable horse is still on his way to becoming a dressage champion after adopting an extraordinary form of equine “braille”. The 15-year-old Appaloosa named Milo, has awed spectators since returning to the show ring last year despite losing sight in both eyes due to a devastating eye condition. The 16-hand gelding […] The post Blind Dressage Horse Wins Competitions By Using ‘Equine Braille’ appeared first on Good News Network .
global_silver_linings.reason: A blind dressage horse competing — and winning — by responding to subtle tactile cues from his rider is a quiet, extraordinary testament to the depth of trust that can exist between human and animal. It's a reminder that limitation and grace can coexist in the most beautiful ways.

discovery_articles.title: Oshirado in Tōno City, Japan
discovery_articles.snippet: Even in Japan, home of the Eight Million Gods, Oshira-sama is an oddity. A tutelary deity of silk, horses, and agriculture, the god continues to be worshipped mainly in rural villages in the northern regions and is typically represented by a pair of mulberry-wood dolls wearing rag hoods. According to the standard myth, Oshira-sama is a pair of male and female deities, the former often taking the form of a horse.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Oshira-sama is worshipped as a pair of mulberry-wood dolls dressed in layered rag hoods — each new cloth added by a devotee, never removed, so the dolls grow fatter with prayer over the years. In a country with eight million gods, this one is still considered strange.

discovery_articles.title: Puppet Center in Alcorcón, Spain
discovery_articles.snippet: The Puppet Center is located in Alcorcón (Madrid) and began its activity in December 2021. The center is managed by the Fundación el Arte del Títere, which is made up of professionals of recognized prestige in the universe of puppet, visual and object theater, and has the collaboration of the Alcorcón City Council. The El Arte del Títere Foundation is the founder and promoter of the Puppet Center.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A center dedicated entirely to the art of puppetry quietly opened in a Madrid suburb in 2021 — proof that the oldest form of theater is still finding new homes. Sometimes the most serious artists work with the smallest hands.

discovery_articles.title: Humansdorp Museum in Humansdorp, South Africa
discovery_articles.snippet: The Humansdorp Museum preserves everyday objects from the town’s early history, some dating back to its founding in 1849, when Matthys Gerhardus Human donated part of his farm Rheboksfontein for the construction of a Dutch Reformed Church. The collection focuses on domestic life rather than grand events. Visitors can grind coffee beans by hand, type a letter on a working typewriter, and browse household items from the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A town named after a man who simply gave away part of his farm now preserves the quiet texture of the lives that followed — coffee grinders, typewriters, the unheroic stuff of daily existence. It's a museum that trusts ordinary things to carry the weight of history.

discovery_articles.title: Clifford Castle in Clifford, England
discovery_articles.snippet: If you ever find yourself in western Herefordshire right by the Welsh border, you might chance upon an eerie, ruined castle on a massive mound known as a motte. The history of the castle is extensive, going back to a time when England was under Norman control. In 1070, William FitzOsbern, the 1st Earl of Hereford, constructed an early motte-and-bailey castle known today as Clifford Castle atop a cliff overlooking a ford on the River Wye.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Clifford Castle has been a ruin so long that it feels less like a collapsed building and more like something the hill itself grew. It's the kind of place where the border between England and Wales feels genuinely negotiable — as it once very dangerously was.

featured_read.title: Swimming and the Meaning of Life
featured_read.snippet: One of my earliest and most vivid childhood memories is of swimming in a cool pool bounded by boulders in the middle of a river in the mountains of Bulgaria, the late-afternoon sun casting komorebi on the water through the rustling leaves. I can still hear the feeling-tone in my body, the strange and lovely simultaneity of absolute presence and absolute peace. I didn’t yet know the word for transcendence.
featured_read.blurb: Maria Popova traces the thread from a childhood river in Bulgaria to the philosophy of transcendence, asking what it means that a body submerged in water can feel, before it has language for it, like the closest thing to eternity. Set aside a quiet half-hour and let this one get you a little wet.

garden_note.note: August evenings in Zürich have that particular quality of warmth that lingers well past supper — the dahlias are coming into their own now, and the kitchen garden is at its most generous, heavy with courgettes you really should have picked yesterday. There's a gentle urgency to late summer: the light is still long, but you can feel it beginning to gather itself.
